lesson.title: Finding Your Way Back: What Makes a Loop
lesson.summary: A loop is any closed path traced through a circuit's branches and nodes that returns to its starting point without revisiting a node, and every loop obeys Kirchhoff's Voltage Law.
lesson.body:
A loop is any closed path you can trace through a circuit, moving from node to node along branches, that eventually returns to the node where you started without passing through any other node twice. It is a purely topological idea, defined only by how the wires and branches connect, not by which components happen to sit on which branch. Loops matter because Kirchhoff's Voltage Law, KVL, applies to every single one of them: no matter which closed path you trace, the sum of the voltage rises and drops around that path must equal zero. That gives you real freedom when analyzing a circuit. You are not stuck with one correct path, you can choose whichever loop makes the algebra easiest, and KVL will still hold exactly.

Consider the simplest possible loop: a 12V battery in series with a 3 ohm resistor R1 and a 1 ohm resistor R2, with nothing else connected. There is exactly one loop here, formed by the two resistors and the battery together. Applying Ohm's law to the whole loop, the current is I = V divided by the total resistance, or 12V divided by 4 ohm, which is 3A. The voltage drop across R1 is I times R1, so 3A times 3 ohm equals 9V, and across R2 it is 3A times 1 ohm, or 3V. Walking around the loop and adding signed voltages: negative 12V for the source, plus 9V, plus 3V, sums to 0V, exactly as KVL requires.

Real circuits usually offer more than one loop to choose from. Take a circuit with two nodes, call them A and B, and three branches connecting them. Branch 1 carries a 10V source in series with a 2 ohm resistor. Branch 2 is just a 4 ohm resistor. Branch 3 is a 2 ohm resistor. Because all three branches share the same two end nodes, you can trace at least three distinct loops: one through branch 1 and branch 2, one through branch 2 and branch 3, and one through branch 1 and branch 3, which steps entirely over branch 2. Every one of these qualifies as a genuine loop, since each starts and ends at the same node and never revisits a node along the way, even the one that skips the middle branch.

Not all of those loops carry independent information, though. With B equal to 3 branches and N equal to 2 nodes, the number of independent loops in this circuit is L = B minus N plus 1, which is 3 minus 2 plus 1, or 2. The third loop, the one that steps over branch 2, is not new information: its KVL equation turns out to be exactly the sum of the other two, so tracing it tells you nothing you could not already get by combining the first pair. This distinction, between a loop in general and a loop that earns its own independent equation, is exactly what the next chapter's idea of a mesh sharpens into a precise, practical rule.

Recognizing loops reliably is the first real analytical payoff of understanding branches and circuit topology. Once you can trace closed paths through a network with confidence and trust that KVL holds on every single one, you have the raw material for every loop based technique that follows, including the mesh current method covered next.
